title: No Priors Ep. 107 | With Physical Intelligence Co-Founder Chelsea Finn
question: In robotic manipulation, how necessary are specialized tactile sensors compared to standard camera setups?
guest: So we've gotten very far just with vision, with RGB images even, and we typically will have one or multiple external base cameras that are looking at the scene and also cameras mounted to each of the wrists of the robot. We can get very far with that. I would love if we could give our robot skin. Unfortunately, a lot of the tactile sensors that are out there are either far less robust than skin, far more expensive, or very low resolution, so there are a lot of challenges on the hardware side there. And we found that mounting RGB cameras to the wrists ends up being very helpful and probably giving you a lot of the same information that tactile sensors can give you.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
It depends on the task: tactile sensors are rarely strictly necessary, but they matter a great deal in a specific class of problems.

For most pick-and-place, sorting, and many everyday household tasks, cameras alone, often with a wrist-mounted camera, are sufficient. Much of the recent progress in imitation learning and vision-language-action models (ALOHA, Diffusion Policy, RT-2, π0) used only vision and proprioception, even for fairly dexterous tasks like folding laundry. Vision can also infer contact indirectly, by watching objects deform or slip.

Touch becomes valuable when vision is occluded or uninformative. Typical cases are in-hand manipulation where the fingers block the view, tight-tolerance insertion, handling fragile or deformable objects that need force regulation, slip detection, and working with transparent items or in the dark. Sensors like GelSight or DIGIT measurably improve success rates in these settings, and simpler force-torque or motor-current sensing often covers part of the gap.

The practical costs are real: tactile sensors are fragile, wear out, lack standardization, and are harder to simulate and collect data for at scale.

Overall, vision is the default, and touch is a complement for contact-rich, precision work, likely more important as robots approach human-level dexterity.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Specialized tactile sensors are optional for most everyday robotic manipulation, where standard external and wrist-mounted cameras prove remarkably sufficient, but they become indispensable in occluded, delicate, or force-critical tasks. Modern visuomotor policies show that multi-view cameras enable complex dexterous skills, such as folding laundry or bimanual assembly, by inferring contact indirectly from object motion and compliant gripper deformation, avoiding the cost, wear, and calibration overhead of tactile hardware. However, vision breaks down when the line of sight is blocked, such as reaching into bags or cluttered bins, or when physical interactions produce no visible cue before failure. Tactile sensors excel here by providing high-frequency, local measurements of normal and shear forces, incipient slip, surface texture, and compliance right at the contact interface. This makes them essential for handling fragile items without crushing or dropping them, performing sub-millimeter insertions, and grasping transparent objects that confound cameras. Ultimately, cameras handle broad spatial guidance and general manipulation, while tactile sensors serve as vital complements for fine, contact-rich control.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
For most manipulation tasks, dedicated tactile sensors aren't strictly needed, but for a large set of contact-heavy tasks they help a lot. Vision-only systems such as RT-2, π0, Diffusion Policy and ALOHA-style teleoperation do pick-and-place, folding and many household tasks well. They work by learning from big demonstration datasets and inferring contact from what they see, often from wrist cameras, and sometimes using joint torque or motor current as a stand-in for touch.

Cameras struggle where contact matters most. The fingers block the view at the moment of grasping, and cameras can't directly measure slip, force or small shifts in pose. Tasks like tight-tolerance insertion, handling fragile or slippery objects, in-hand reorientation, cable routing and sensing an object's texture or firmness benefit clearly from tactile input. Visuotactile sensors like GelSight, DIGIT and GelSlim, and policies that combine vision and touch, consistently do better in these cases. Touch can also save data, because a policy no longer has to infer forces from pixels.

Cost, durability, calibration, wear and differences between individual sensors still hold back wider use. The emerging consensus is that touch is optional for coarse tasks, close to essential for dexterous ones, and most valuable alongside vision rather than as a replacement for it.

They also provide direct, high-frequency feedback for incipient slip detection, tight-tolerance insertion, and delicate force regulation that vision can only infer indirectly after an error has already occurred.

In practice, cameras serve as the default foundation for general manipulation, while tactile sensing is a high-value complement—necessary primarily for contact-rich, precision, or occluded tasks where visual feedback hits hard physical limits.
